overview.label: Overview
overview.heading: One record for every deal
paras: The Deals module is where a Kelp user works a deal from first look to investment committee. Each company gets a single record: a one-pager with what the company does and why it matters, the deal size and a score, the IC notes, the valuation, and every report and document the team has gathered.

We designed the module around how deal teams actually move: scan the pipeline, open a company, read the one-pager, compare it with similar companies, and prepare for the committee, without leaving the workspace or rebuilding the same summary in a slide deck.

problemStatement: How might we give a deal team one trustworthy record per company, so the one-pager, the IC notes, the numbers and the documents never live in five different places again?

empathy.heading: Who we designed for
empathy.intro: Private-markets teams evaluate many companies at once, under deadlines, with information arriving from bankers, founders, data providers and their own diligence.

people.context: Build and maintain the company one-pager, add notes from calls, and pull financials together for the committee.
Need the essentials of a deal in a minute: what the company does, the size, the score, and what the team thinks.
Needs comparable information across companies, in the same structure every time.

painPoints: Deal information was scattered across email, spreadsheets, shared drives and slide decks.
Every company summary was rebuilt by hand, in a slightly different format each time.
Comparing two or three companies meant copying numbers into a new spreadsheet.
IC notes, valuations and diligence reports were hard to find once a deal moved on.

items.title: A lot of data on one screen
items.body: A single deal carries a description, differentiators, founders and shareholders, geographic focus, financials, scores, notes, tasks and documents. All of it matters, and none of it can hide.

items.title: Consistency across companies
items.body: A one-pager is only useful to a committee if every company is described in the same structure, so the team can read across deals rather than decode each summary.

items.title: Comparison without spreadsheets
items.body: Teams regularly weigh similar companies against each other. The product had to make that comparison a view, not a side project in Excel.

steps.title: Map the deal lifecycle
steps.body: We mapped how a company moves from sourcing to the investment committee and what the team needs at each step. That gave us the record structure: a one-pager first, then valuation, IC notes, post-deal notes, activity, tasks and documents.

steps.title: Design the one-pager
steps.body: We designed a fixed one-pager structure, product or service, key differentiator, customer value proposition, founders, top shareholders, geographic focus and key markets, so every company reads the same way.

steps.title: Make comparison a view
steps.body: We built a compare view that lines up selected companies on score, sector, founding year, shareholders and key financials such as revenue, EBITDA, ROCE and ROE, so the team can read across deals in one table.

steps.title: Share one design system
steps.body: Tables, tags, scores and navigation were designed as shared components, so the deals module, the plugin and the investor portal feel like one product.

solution.label: The experience we created
solution.heading: From pipeline to investment committee
paras: A deals workspace where the pipeline, each company's record and the comparison between companies sit side by side, with the documents and notes that support every decision one click away.

items.title: Company one-pager

items.title: Side-by-side comparison

items.title: Deal list with context

items.title: IC notes and valuation
items.body: Committee notes and valuation work live on the deal record, next to the information they refer to.

items.title: Activity, notes and tasks
items.body: Interactions, notes, tasks and documents are attached to the company, so context survives handovers.

items.title: Sourcing detail
items.body: Summary, financials, leadership, culture and digital presence, organised under a sourcing section of the record.

faq.q: What is the Kelp deals module?
faq.a: A deals workspace for private-markets investment teams: every company's one-pager, IC notes, valuation and documents in one place, and companies compared side by side.

faq.q: What problem did the Kelp deals module solve?
faq.a: A single deal carries a description, differentiators, founders and shareholders, geographic focus, financials, scores, notes, tasks and documents. All of it matters, and none of it can hide. The question we set out to answer: How might we give a deal team one trustworthy record per company, so the one-pager, the IC notes, the numbers and the documents never live in five different places again?

faq.q: How did Designit approach the Kelp deals module?
faq.a: We worked in 4 phases: Map the deal lifecycle; design the one-pager; make comparison a view; share one design system. We mapped how a company moves from sourcing to the investment committee and what the team needs at each step.

faq.q: What should deal management software for private equity include?
faq.a: A single record per company that the whole team trusts: a consistent one-pager, the investment committee notes, valuation, documents, activity and tasks, plus a way to compare companies without exporting to a spreadsheet. That is the structure we designed for Kelp.

faq.q: What is a company one-pager in private equity?
faq.a: A short, standardised summary of a company used to screen and discuss deals: what it does, why it is different, who founded and owns it, where it operates and the key numbers. Standardising it is what lets a committee read across deals.

faq.q: How do you design data-dense screens for analysts?
faq.a: Keep the structure fixed and the hierarchy clear: the same sections in the same order on every record, the few numbers that matter given the most visual weight, and everything else one click away rather than hidden.

faq.q: How do you design a comparison table that people actually use?
faq.a: Compare only what drives the decision, in rows people already think in: score, sector, ownership and the key financials. Kelp's compare view lines up selected companies in one table instead of a separate spreadsheet.

faq.q: What was the hardest part of designing for investment teams?
faq.a: Communicating complex data clearly. Kelp's Head of CX described the work as simplifying and communicating complex data through tables, graphs and visualisations.

faq.q: How long does a Designit engagement take?
faq.a: A Design Sprint is delivered in 5 business days. Full product design engagements run 4–12 weeks depending on scope. Monthly retainers are ongoing, with one active request at a time and a 24-hour response time.

faq.q: Which regions does Designit work with?
faq.a: Designit is based in Noida, India, and works with clients in India and the UAE; we also take on projects for teams in the United States and the United Kingdom. All communication is in English, and invoices are in the client's market currency: INR in India, USD in the US, GBP in the UK, and USD or AED in the UAE. Working hours overlap with EST and PST for US teams and with GMT for UK teams, so scheduled calls land inside a normal working day on both sides.

faq.q: Who actually works on the engagement?
faq.a: Senior practitioners, from kickoff through to developer handoff. There are no account managers in the middle, no junior hand-offs once a contract is signed, and no offshore layer. Clients talk directly to the people producing the work, which is what keeps the feedback loop short enough to ship in days rather than weeks.

faq.q: What tools does the studio work in?
faq.a: Figma is the primary canvas, with prototyping in Figma or Protopie and engineering handoff through Figma Dev Mode. Research runs on Maze and Hotjar. Project tracking sits in Notion or Linear, and teams are welcome to work inside their own stack instead.

faq.q: What are the engagement models and what do they cost?
faq.a: Three models. A Sprint is a fixed scope delivered in five business days. A monthly retainer covers one active request at a time with a 24-hour response window, priced by the time it needs. A full end-to-end engagement runs four to twelve weeks depending on scope. A tailored quote follows within 24 hours of a discovery call.

faq.q: Which sectors has the studio shipped work in?
faq.a: Six: B2B SaaS and enterprise tooling, EdTech and digital learning, Fintech and Web3, luxury real estate and PropTech, e-commerce and retail, and automotive HMI. Shipped work includes Adda247, StudyIQ, Tata Elxsi, Kelp Global, Betacrew, Omniyat and LIV Residences.
